651: The skill of support yields only wealth. The skill of action yields everything desired.
652: Ministers should always avoid acts that bring fame now but no benefit later.
653: Those who say "we will become better" must avoid acts that destroy their name.
654: Those of infallible judgment will not repeat the disgraced deeds of former ministers, however great the peril.
655: Never do what you will grieve over saying "what have I done." If done, it were good to grieve not.
656: Even if his mother starves, a minister must never do what the wise despise.
657: The wise person's deepest poverty is worth more than riches heaped by wrongdoing.
658: The deeds of those who do what the great forbid bring sorrow, even when they succeed.
659: What is gained with tears to the victim departs with tears to oneself. What is gained fairly bears fruit in the end.
660: Guarding power with dirty money is like holding a wet clay pot together by filling it with water.
661: Firmness in action is simply firmness of mind. All else is not that.
662: The wise hold two rules: never do what ruins, and never sink when ruin comes.
663: True manliness completes a deed before publishing it. Announcing it beforehand brings sorrow beyond remedy.
664: Anyone can say how a thing should be done. It is far harder to do what has been said.
665: Counsel that proves itself in success wins everyone's esteem.
666: If those who plan possess firmness in executing, they obtain what they desired, exactly as they desired it.
667: Despise no one for their size. On the little linchpin the great chariot turns.
668: What has been firmly resolved must be as firmly carried out, without delay.
669: Though it pains at the outset, do with firmness the act that yields bliss at the end.
670: The great do not esteem those without firmness in action, whatever else those people may have.
671: Consultation ends in a resolution. Delay in executing that resolve is itself an evil.
672: Sleep over the things that can wait. Never sleep over the things that cannot.
673: When overcoming your enemy is possible, fighting is good. When it is not, try a surer method.
674: A half-done task and a lingering feud are live coals — they smolder and destroy.
675: Do a deed only after weighing five things: money, means, time, execution, and place.
676: Perform an act after considering the effort required, the obstacles to meet, and the great profit on completion.
677: Once begun, the method is this: learn the mind of the one who knows the secret of the task.
678: To use one undertaking to accomplish another like it is like catching one wild elephant with another.
679: Win your enemy's enemy before you court your friend.
680: The small, guarding their frightened people, accept peace when the strong offer it.
681: An ambassador needs affection for his own, fitting birth, and qualities pleasing to royalty.
682: Love for his sovereign, knowledge of his affairs, and discriminating speech before other rulers — an ambassador's three essentials.
683: Power in politics among the learned — that is the mark of the ambassador's speech.
684: He may go on a mission who combines three things: natural sense, an attractive presence, and well-tested learning.
685: The ambassador speaks briefly, avoids harshness, talks so rulers smile — and brings good to his sovereign.
686: The ambassador has studied politics, talks impressively, does not flinch at angry looks, and knows the art fit for the time.
687: Chief of ambassadors: he who knows the decorum, the occasion, the place, and delivers the message in due measure.
688: The faithful messenger's qualifications: purity, the support of ministers abroad, boldness — and truthfulness beyond the three.
689: Fit alone to carry the reply is he whose firmness will not let slip even a word that shames his sovereign.
690: The true ambassador seeks his sovereign's good fearlessly, though the message should cost him his life.
691: Let all who serve under a warrior king's roof act so.
692: The minister who hides nothing from his king gains everlasting fortune through him.
693: Ministers who would save themselves avoid serious errors — once a king's suspicion is roused, none can remove it.
694: In the sovereign's presence, ministers should neither whisper to others nor smile at them.
695: While the king is in secret counsel, listen to nothing, pry with no questions — wait to hear what is later divulged.
696: Read the king's mood, pick the right time, and suggest what is desirable — pleasantly.
697: Give agreeable advice always, but never recommend a useless act, though asked.
698: Honor the divine light in your king. Never sneer, "he is younger than us, kin of our kin."
699: The wise will not do wrong to please even a king.
700: The foolish claim "we are old friends" that leads a minister into unseemly acts will ruin him.
701: The minister who reads the king's mind by a look, unasked, is a perpetual ornament to the world girt by the never-drying sea.
702: He is to be esteemed a god who can tell without doubt what is within another's mind.
703: A ruler should shower gifts on the one who can read other minds — reading his own.
704: Those who read thoughts unspoken and those who cannot may look alike in body — in mind they are different.
705: Of what use are eyes among one's members, if they cannot read another's by their own?
706: As the mirror reflects what is near, the face shows what is uppermost in the mind.
707: Is anything so full of knowledge as the face? It runs ahead of the mind, whether pleased or vexed.
708: If a ruler gains those who read his face and lift what weighs on it, it is enough for him to look at them.
709: With ministers who read the eye, even a foreign king's eyes betray his hate or friendship.
710: Those who boast of sharpness have one measuring-rod: their own eyes, nothing more.
711: Let the pure who know the arrangement of words speak with deliberation, after reading the assembly before them.
712: Let the good who know the worth of words speak with clear knowledge, after weighing the fit time.
713: Whoever speaks without reading the room knows neither words nor learning.
714: Be a light in a wise assembly; wear the quiet white of plaster among fools.
715: The modesty that does not rush to speak among superiors is the best of all good qualities.
716: To blunder before the deeply learned is like a good soul stumbling off the good path.
717: The learning of those who have read and understood shines in an assembly that weighs words faultlessly.
718: Lecturing the self-taught is watering plants that grow by themselves.
719: Never let your best words slip, forgetfully, before the wrong assembly.
720: To utter a fine word in an assembly of the inferior is like dropping nectar on the ground.
721: Those who know words and the room will not falter before the powerful.
722: Those who can pleasantly set forth their learning before the learned are counted the most learned among the learned.
723: Many can die fearlessly before their foes. Few are fearless in an assembly of the learned.
724: Speak your learning before the learned, and leave having learned more.
725: To reply fearlessly before a foreign court, learn the logic of words by the rules.
726: What use is a sword to the faint-hearted — or learning to those afraid of a clever hall?
727: The shy scholar's learning is a bright sword in a hand too weak to draw it.
728: Those who cannot speak well before a good assembly are unprofitable despite all their learning.
729: Those who have learned and understood yet fear the assembly of the good rank below the unlettered.
730: Those who through fear of the assembly cannot present their learning well are like the dead, though alive.
731: A kingdom is that where tillers of the land and the virtuous flourish together.
732: A kingdom is that desired for immense wealth, growing ever in prosperity, free of destructive causes.
733: A kingdom is that which bears any burden pressed upon it and still pays its full tribute.
734: A kingdom is that which continues free of famine, incurable epidemics, and destructive foes.
735: A kingdom is that without feuding factions, traitors within, or savages harassing the throne.
736: The learned say the best kingdom knows no evil from foes — and, if injured, suffers no loss of fruitfulness.
737: A kingdom's constituents: the two waters — rain and springs — well-placed hills, and an indestructible fort.
738: Freedom from epidemics, wealth, produce, happiness, and protection — these five are a kingdom's ornaments.
739: The best kingdom's wealth flows without toil. One that toils for every coin is not yet a kingdom.
740: All the excellences above are of no use to a country without harmony between ruler and ruled.
741: A fort serves those who march out to war and those who run to it for refuge.
742: A fort is that which has everlasting water, open plains, hills, and cool shady forests.
743: The learned say a fortress is an enclosure of four qualities: height, breadth, strength, and inaccessibility.
744: A fort is that with wide space within but few places to guard — such that it breaks the courage of besiegers.
745: A fort is that which cannot be taken, abounds in provisions, and gives its people an easy defense.
746: A fort is that which has all needful things and excellent heroes to defend it from destruction.
747: A fort is that which cannot be captured by blockade, assault, or undermining.
748: That is a fort whose people can overcome even abler besiegers without losing ground.
749: A fort derives its excellence from the stratagems its people devise to defeat enemies in the field.
750: A perfect fort is as nothing if its defenders are not themselves excellent in action.
751: Besides wealth there is nothing that can lift people of no importance into importance.
752: The poor are despised by all; the rich are praised by all.
753: Wealth is a light that travels where you send it and burns away enmity.
754: Wealth acquired with knowledge of the right means and without foul practices yields virtue and happiness.
755: Avoid rather than seek the accumulation of wealth that does not flow in with mercy and love.
756: Even the wealth of defeated foes enters the ruler's treasury.
757: Mercy is the child of love — and wealth is the nurse that rears it.
758: With wealth in hand, any undertaking is like watching an elephant-fight from a hill — safe and clear.
759: Accumulate wealth: it destroys the arrogance of your foes. No weapon is sharper.
760: For those who have honestly gained abundance, the other two — virtue and pleasure — are easy to gain.
761: An army complete in all its parts, conquering without fear of wounds, is the ruler's chief wealth.
762: Only a veteran army stands by its king in defeat — fearless of wounds, unmindful of losses.
763: What if hostile rats roar like the sea? They perish at the mere breath of the cobra.
764: That indeed is an army which has stood firm of old, without destruction or desertion.
765: That indeed is an army which can resist united, even if the God of Death advances in fury.
766: Valour, honour, a proud lineage of deeds, and trustworthiness — these guard an army.
767: An army is one that can meet the foe's advancing dust-cloud, knowing how to ward off the coming clash.
768: An army short of valour may still win fame by the splendor of its bearing.
769: An army triumphs while free of losses, feuds, and want.
770: However many soldiers an army holds, without generals it will not last.
771: Foes, do not face my chief. Many who did now stand as statues.
772: Better to hold the spear that missed an elephant than the one that felled a hare.
773: Fierceness against a foe is great valour. To lift up a fallen foe is valour's height.
774: The hero, lance buried in his own body, will pluck it out and laugh.
775: For the valiant, to blink before a thrown spear is already defeat.
776: The hero counts every unwounded day a wasted day.
777: To those who seek renown above life itself, the prisoner's shackle is an adornment.
778: The heroes who do not fear losing their lives will not cool their ardour even when the king forbids their fighting.
779: Who would call it failure — those who seal their oath with their death?
780: A death that fills a ruler's eyes with tears is worth obtaining even by begging.
